findings.claim: The Catechism (CCC 2266) identifies the primary purposes as: protecting society from harmful acts, preserving public order, and providing for the amendment (reform) of the offender.
findings.truth: CCC 2266 states that punishment "has the primary aim of redressing the disorder introduced by the offense". Defending public order, protecting people's safety and the medicinal purpose of correcting the offender are named as additional aims, not the primary one. The lesson drops the retributive primary aim and promotes the secondary aims in its place - the exact point the spec examines under 'the different rationales given for criminal penalties: retribution, deterrence, rehabilitation'.
findings.evidence: vatican.va Catechism 2266 (Part 3, Section 2, Article 5); spec p.55 Theme 4 'Crime and Punishment'

findings.claim: Augustine, in his letters to Macedonius (Letters 134 and 153), argued that the state could rightly execute criminals and that doing so could even be an act of mercy - preventing further sin. (Repeated in practice_questions[4].marks, practice_questions[5].marks and flashcard_questions[9].)
findings.truth: The spec names these letters (Letter 134(4) and 153(3)) as evidence for the development of Catholic teaching on capital punishment. In those letters Augustine is writing to Roman officials to plead for clemency: he accepts that the state has the right to punish, but he asks the official NOT to execute the condemned so that they may repent and be corrected. Presenting execution itself as Augustine's 'act of mercy' inverts the argument of the very sections the spec cites. Options: (a) rewrite to 'Augustine accepted that the state had the right to punish, including by death, but in these letters he begged the authorities to spare condemned criminals so that they had time to repent' - the reading standard in Catholic GCSE texts; (b) leave as is if a source is found showing the mercy-through-execution argument in Letters 134/153. I could not confirm either reading from the allowed sources (Wikipedia has no Augustine section on capital punishment; wikisource 404). Recommend (a).
findings.evidence: spec p.55 Theme 4 cites 'St Augustine, Letter 134(4) & 153 (3) to Macedonius'; external confirmation unavailable within the permitted hosts
findings.ruling: Clemency reading applied in prose and flashcard.

findings.claim: The Catechism (CCC 1033) states that hell is not God's will for anyone: "God predestines no one to go to hell."
findings.truth: That sentence is CCC 1037, not CCC 1033. CCC 1033 defines hell as definitive self-exclusion from communion with God. A wrong paragraph number costs the mark when the question asks for a named source.
findings.evidence: vatican.va Catechism 1033-1037 (fetched; 1037 carries the sentence verbatim)

findings.claim: Flashcard [4].q: "What does CCC 1033 say about God's role in hell?"
findings.truth: Same wrong paragraph as F3. It should be CCC 1037.

findings.claim: (CCC 1257-1261 - the principle of "subsistit in" and the broader understanding of implicit faith)
findings.truth: "Subsistit in" comes from Lumen Gentium 8 and is treated in CCC 816 and 870. CCC 1257-1261 are about the necessity of baptism: God has bound salvation to baptism but is not himself bound by his sacraments, and a person who seeks the truth and does God's will as they understand it can be saved. The label attached to the paragraph range is wrong.

findings.claim: practice_questions[5].marks: "John Paul II's Evangelii Gaudium and Pope Francis's emphasis on God's universal mercy are part of the ordinary Magisterium's ongoing affirmation..."
findings.truth: Evangelii Gaudium (2013) is Pope Francis's apostolic exhortation, not John Paul II's. The spec names it as a Pope Francis document. John Paul II's encyclical on this course is Evangelium Vitae (1995) - the two titles are already confusable, so the mark scheme teaches the confusion.
findings.evidence: spec p.56 'Pope Francis' Evangelii Gaudium 15, 48-49, 197-198, 264-265'; lesson 3 of this unit dates it correctly to 2013

findings.claim: as both the Body of Christ (CCC 1 Corinthians 12) and the People of God
findings.truth: 1 Corinthians 12 is scripture, not a Catechism paragraph. The reference should read (1 Corinthians 12); the lesson body cites it correctly.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency with content_html paragraph n12

findings.claim: "the presence of G-d's grace", "through which G-d communicates saving grace", "not a barrier to G-d but the very medium through which G-d is encountered", and the data-def "Catholics receive G-d's forgiveness".
findings.truth: G-d is the Jewish convention for avoiding writing the divine name. It has no place in a Catholic theology lesson, and the same lesson writes "God" everywhere else, including in the prose sentence next to the affected data-def. It reads as an error to any student and mixes the wrong tradition into a Catholic paper.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency within lesson 3 content_html and its glossary_terms

findings.claim: Matthew 6:14-15 quoted as "...but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses."
findings.truth: The quotation blends two translations: NRSV verse 15 reads "but if you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses"; "their trespasses" is the RSV/KJV wording, which uses "men" not "others". The sense is unchanged, so no mark is at risk.

findings.claim: The revision tip asks students to "give one idea from each of these Evangelii Gaudium passages: 15, 48-49, 197-198, 264-265" and the exam tip cites Evangelii Gaudium 15, but the lesson never explains paragraph 15. It teaches paragraph 83 and paragraphs 14-18 instead.
findings.truth: The spec names paragraphs 15, 48-49, 197-198 and 264-265. Paragraph 83 and 14-18 are accurate in themselves (83 is the 'tomb psychology' passage; 14-18 sets out the settings of the new evangelisation), so nothing taught is wrong - but paragraph 15, which the spec does name, is asked for and never covered.

findings.claim: Flashcard [11]: "What is the Natural Law basis for Catholic opposition to capital punishment?" answered with "Every person bears the 'imago Dei' - a dignity that cannot be forfeited even by serious crime."
findings.truth: Imago Dei is a scriptural and theological ground (Genesis 1:26-27), not strictly a Natural Law argument. Natural Law would argue from the primary precept of preserving life. The answer is defensible but does not answer the question as asked.
findings.evidence: CCC 2267 revised text; Aquinas on the primary precepts

findings.claim: Flashcard [2]: "What are 'deterrence' and 'rehabilitation' as purposes of punishment (CCC 2266)?"
findings.truth: CCC 2266 names correction of the guilty party (rehabilitation), defence of public order and protection of people's safety, but it does not name deterrence. Deterrence is a standard rationale for the topic, just not one CCC 2266 supplies.

summary: Eight fixable errors across all three lessons: a misstated CCC 2266 on the aims of punishment, CCC 1037 cited as CCC 1033 twice, 'subsistit in' pinned to the wrong paragraph range, Evangelii Gaudium attributed to John Paul II in a mark scheme, a garbled 'CCC 1 Corinthians 12' reference, and the Jewish 'G-d' convention left in four places in a Catholic lesson. Practice-question forms are correct Eduqas shape (2/2/5/5/8/15), the board is never named, and the 2021 census figures, CCC 2267 (2018) quotation, Evangelium Vitae 56 and all knowledge-check answer keys are right. One ADJUDICATE: Augustine's letters to Macedonius are presented as arguing that execution could be an act of mercy, which inverts the clemency plea in the sections the spec cites.
